query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the material’s ability to develop a mechanically stable, passivating oxide film along its grain boundaries. This film limits the extent of corrosion damage and distributes mechanical stresses during wear, resulting in a synergistic reduction of both degradation processes.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform high-entropy alloy microstructure produced under standard processing conditions, with a random solid-solution structure and minimal pre‐existing passivating grain boundary films.
generation.intervention: Prepare a controlled set of high-entropy alloy samples using two different processing routes: one optimized to promote grain boundary passivation (e.g., via controlled oxidation or heat-treatment conditions to encourage oxide film formation) and a second following a conventional process that does not promote such film formation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a harsh corrosive environment (e.g., a salt solution) combined with a controlled mechanical wear regime (cyclic loading or abrasive wear) in a quasi-simultaneous manner.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries decorated by a thin, mechanically-stable passivating oxide film.
generation.mechanism: The passivating film acts as a barrier to corrosive attack while also distributing mechanical stresses during wear, lowering the localized degradation rate. In contrast, samples without the film experience accelerated chemical erosion at wear-induced damaged sites, where fresh reactive surfaces are continuously exposed.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with enhanced grain boundary passivation will show a lower overall degradation rate under combined wear and corrosive conditions compared to the baseline. Specifically, both the individual measures of wear (reduced wear depth or volume loss) and corrosion (slower corrosion rate) will exhibit synergistic improvement, such that the combined effect is less severe than would be expected by adding the independent effects alone.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloys processed via conventional methods that do not encourage the development of a passivating grain boundary oxide film.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in corrosive and mechanical loading conditions that are moderate enough to allow the film to remain intact. The mechanism may fail under extreme wear (overwhelming the film’s mechanical integrity) or in environments where the chemical aggressiveness exceeds the film’s protective capability.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative contributions of the oxide film to reducing wear-corrosion synergy and the precise threshold conditions (mechanical load and corrosive aggressiveness) for film failure are presently uncertain due to a lack of detailed prior quantification in similar high-entropy alloy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled experiment by fabricating two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set processed to promote grain boundary passivation and a control set processed conventionally. Subject both sets to identical exposures in a salt solution environment while applying cyclic mechanical wear. Monitor the evolution of surface degradation over time.
measurements: Measure wear depth and material loss using profilometry
Determine corrosion rates via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
Assess microstructural changes and oxide film presence using SEM/TEM and XPS analyses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with promoted grain boundary passivation do not demonstrate a significantly reduced overall degradation (i.e., both lower wear and lower corrosion rates) relative to the control samples, or if the behavior of the combined degradation deviates from a synergistic improvement predicted by the presence of the oxide film, the hypothesis will be falsified.
